name: Ecru-Olive
lede: Ecru-Olive is a muted tan-olive that shares its ISCC-NBS block with at least ten other named colors.

sections.title: One block, many names
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature places the swatch at plate XXX, hue 21′′, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 reads it as a dark yellow, under 2 units from the block center, among the closer matches in our library [1]. The same ISCC-NBS region also covers names such as Sudan, Russet Leaf, Middle Stone and Light Yellowish Olive, the last under 1.1 units from this hex [1].

Our library's own nearest match is [[dark-beige]], with [[dark-olive-buff]] and [[water-grey]] close by [1][2]. The name pairs "ecru", an unbleached linen tone, with "olive" [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color, as photographed, appears in 2,718 of 23,781 paintings, about 11.43 percent, more common than 94 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 314 of 3,449 paintings, at 9.1 percent of that period's paintings, 1.3 times the overall rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light [3]. Its most devoted painter is Arnoud van Halen, carrying it in 27 of 50 works here, 5.0 times the baseline for his museums [3]. It is most over-represented in Iran (3.5 times expected; 10 of 29 paintings) [3]. The earliest match in the archive is a 799 painting, 1113 years before the name's 1912 record, so this is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a pigment identification, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].

issues: Fixed: the field-notes paragraph (and the matching "field" object) invented an earliest-match claim ("a Roman funerary portrait from about 25 CE") that doesn't match the real first-seen record (a 799 painting, no painter attributed) and borrowed a Paulus Potter painter stat (13 of 28) that belongs to a different slug (fallen-leaf, 11 of 28) — this slug's real most-devoted painter is Arnoud van Halen (27 of 50, 5.0x). The Iran over-representation count was also off (13 of 29, should be 10 of 29) and the presence count (2,709) didn't exactly match the real count (2,718 as-photographed). Rewrote the paragraph directly from data/graph/fieldnotes for this slug; removed every unsupported claim rather than inventing a replacement for it.
